catalog_quote: Shanjo and Fwe have an identical 5 vowel system, i.e. /i e a o u/, without distinctive vowel length, but with automatic penultimate vowel lengthening in citation forms or phrase-finally. [...] The tone systems of Shanjo and Fwe have not been studied in detail yet, but they seem to be quite similar at first sight. The basic tones in both languages are high and low, but high can be realized falling on the penultimate syllable of words in isolation or in phrase-final position. More details and examples follow in subsection 3.11. [...] As regards Shanjo and Fwe, I have not yet undertaken a detailed study of their tone system, but a first analysis of my lexical data allows identifying the basic tone patterns for nouns and verbs in isolation. [...] Among disyllabic noun stems in citation form, only three distinctive tone schemes can be observed: LL, HL and FL. If there is a noun prefix, it never bears a high tone. [...] As discussed above, both languages manifest automatic penultimate vowel lengthening (27b), another common eastern Bantu phenomenon (Hyman 2003). Such lengthening is often found in association with the leftward shift of a pre-pausal or word-final H to the penult (27c) (Kisseberth & Odden 2003).

PDF page 3 (running head '112') closes section 2 with 'The tone systems of Shanjo a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shanjo is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with no contrastive vowel length; the only prominence-like property reported is automatic lengthening of the penultimate vowel of a word in citation form or phrase-final position, where a H on that penult surfaces as a fall (analysed diachronically as leftward shift of a final H onto the lengthened penult). The author never speaks of stress or accent and gives no word-stress rule; the penult lengthening is positionally (phrase-finally) conditioned.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author notes the tone system 'has not been studied in detail yet'. Noun prefixes never bear H in citation forms (p.122).
new_statements.domain_note: Penultimate lengthening and the falling realization of H are explicitly restricted to citation forms / phrase-final position, i.e. a phrase-level (pre-pausal) phenomenon rather than a word-level stress; statements are made jointly for Shanjo and Zambian Fwe.
new_statements.identity_note: Bostoen 2009 describes Shanjo (K36) as spoken west of the Zambezi between Sioma and Sesheke, Western Province, Zambia, from his own August 2007 fieldwork with two Shanjo consultants; the quoted prosodic statements are made jointly for Shanjo and Zambian Fwe (fwee1238), which he treats as sharing the same vowel/length/tone basics. Glottolog shan1291 was formerly subsumed under ISO toi (Tonga) but is a distinct western Botatwe language closest to Fwe.

new_statements.quote: Although the data is sparse and inconsistent, Bostoen's preliminary survey of diachronic tone shifts produces a phonological change consistently attested within the Kafue languages considered by Bostoen (Tonga, Ila, and Lenje) and not attested in the western Botatwe languages included in Bostoen's analysis (Shanjo and Fwe). Tonga is well-known for its pattern of high tone anticipation in which, with some exceptions, the high tone undergoes a binary leftward shift, moving one syllable, often onto the prefix (Goldsmith 1984:22). Bostoen observes that this shift also occurs in Lenje and Ila (Bostoen 2009:122-3). In contrast, when a word has a prefix in Shanjo or Fwe, it does not bear a high tone (Bostoen, 2009:121). [p.78] ... Both languages exhibit a leftward shift of the word-final high tone (Bostoen 2009: 127). [p.80]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with and derivative of the existing Bostoen 2009 statement (tone language, H and L, no stress statement); adds nothing independent, since every tonal remark is cited from Bostoen 2009 pp.121-127. It confirms that no 'stress' claim exists in this source, so the catalog's tone language, no stress statement reading stands. The 'likely states stress' tag on this work is wrong: it is a lexicostatistical classification paper with no phonological description of Shanjo.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule about word stress is given. The paper treats Shanjo as a tone language (high vs. low tone) and only repeats, second-hand from Bostoen 2009, two diachronic tone facts: a noun prefix in Shanjo/Fwe never carries a high tone, and the word-final high tone has shifted leftward. The words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the 32 pages (one 'accent' hit is a false positive elsewhere in the text search: none in the prosodic sense); penultimate lengthening is not mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Shanjo; footnote 11 (p.78) notes that high-tone anticipation occurs in Zambian Totela but apparently not in Namibian (Caprivi) Totela, a different language
new_statements.identity_note: de Luna 2010 treats Shanjo as a single language (K36, 'Zambezi Hook' branch of Western Botatwe together with Fwe), spoken between Sesheke and Sioma, Western Province, Zambia; no dialect is named. Her phonological remarks come from Bostoen's 2007 Western Province field data, the same variety as the catalog's Bostoen 2009 statement.

sources.note: Sec. 2 (p.111-112): five vowels, no distinctive vowel length, 'automatic penultimate vowel lengthening in citation forms or phrase-finally'; tones H and L, H realized as falling on the penultimate syllable of words in isolation/phrase-final. Sec. 3.11 (p.122) repeats penult lengthening as a common eastern-Bantu trait linked to leftward shift of final H to the penult. The word 'stress' is never used; no word-stress rule stated.

sources.citation: Gunnink, Hilde. 2022. A grammar of Fwe: A Bantu language of Zambia and Namibia (Studies in Diversity Linguistics). Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Describes Fwe, not Shanjo. On Shanjo it says only (p.13 fn.1) 'the available documentation on Shanjo is too limited' and (p.88 fn.2) 'The study of lexical tone in Shanjo by Bostoen (2009) indicates no trace of HTA [high tone anticipation] in this language'; names Bostoen 2009 as the description of the Shanjo phoneme inventory. No stress statement for Shanjo.
